nameStory: The Brown Banded Hermit gets its name from the distinctive brown bands that wrap around its legs like tiny striped socks. This pattern is so unique that it's the only hermit crab along the northeastern U.S. coast with banded legs, making it a standout among its shell-carrying cousins.
description: The Brown Banded Hermit is a small marine hermit crab that lives in borrowed snail shells along the Atlantic coast. Like all hermit crabs, it has a soft, curved abdomen that it protects by backing into empty shells, which it carries around like a mobile home. What makes this species special is the striking brown bands that circle its walking legs, creating a distinctive striped pattern. These crabs are typically small, fitting comfortably in shells about the size of a large marble.

idTips.label: Banded Legs
idTips.description: Look for distinctive brown bands wrapping around the walking legs like striped stockings - this is the only hermit crab in New England with this pattern

idTips.label: Shell Home
idTips.description: Lives in empty snail shells, often moon snail or periwinkle shells, which you'll see moving around with legs and claws poking out

idTips.label: Asymmetrical Claws
idTips.description: The right claw is typically larger than the left and helps seal the shell opening when the crab retreats inside

idTips.label: Quick Movement
idTips.description: Scuttles quickly across tide pools and sandy areas, and will rapidly withdraw into its shell when disturbed with a soft scratching sound

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Small enough to fit in shells ranging from pea-sized to about the diameter of a quarter, making them one of the smaller hermit crabs in the region

habitat: Brown Banded Hermits live in shallow coastal waters along rocky shores, tide pools, and sandy bottoms in the western Atlantic. You'll find them scuttling around in the intertidal zone, particularly in areas with plenty of empty snail shells to choose from as they grow.

seasonality.spring: More active as waters warm, often seen moving between tide pools during low tides, especially on calm days.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to spot during summer months when they're frequently visible in shallow tide pools and along shorelines.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters as temperatures cool, though still findable in protected tide pools.
seasonality.winter: Less active and moved to deeper waters, rarely seen in accessible tide pools during the coldest months.

funFact: When a Brown Banded Hermit outgrows its shell, it will actually line up with other hermit crabs in a 'vacancy chain' - each crab inspecting the next larger shell until they all simultaneously switch homes in a perfectly choreographed housing shuffle!
confusionNotes: The banded legs make this species nearly impossible to confuse with other hermit crabs - if you see stripes on the legs, you've found a Brown Banded Hermit. Other New England hermit crabs like the Long-claw and Flat-clawed have solid-colored legs without any banding pattern.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives the Long-claw Hermit (which has elongated claws) and Flat-clawed Hermit (which has flattened, broad claws), the Brown Banded Hermit has proportionally normal-sized claws but sports those unmistakable brown leg bands. The Acadian Hermit Crab is typically larger and found in deeper waters, while the Brown Banded prefers shallow coastal areas where its distinctive striped pattern is easily visible.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hermit crabs, the Long-claw is distinguished by its notably slender, elongated claws compared to the Flat-clawed Hermit Crab's broad, flattened pincers.

Among New England's hermit crabs, the flat-clawed hermit is unmistakable due to its shield-like claws - the long-claw hermit has thin, extended claws, while the Acadian hermit has more typical rounded pincers.
Compared to its close relative the Long-claw Hermit Crab, the Acadian hermit has a more robust build and prefers colder waters further north.
Among New England's hermit crabs, the hairy hermit is the only one with distinctly fuzzy, bristled legs - its relatives like the Long-claw and Flat-clawed hermit crabs have smooth legs and claws.
